name: AWS Glue
one: Cleans and moves data between places.
like: The kitchen prep station. Wash, chop and arrange before the cooking starts.
what: Glue extracts data, transforms it and loads it somewhere useful. Its catalogue records what your data looks like so Athena and Redshift can read it. It is serverless, so nothing to run.
nope: A single simple copy job. A script may be enough.
pay: Per data processing unit hour.
eg: Nightly job turning raw CSV exports into clean Parquet for Athena.

name: Amazon Athena
one: Run SQL directly on files sitting in S3.
like: Reading the files in your cupboard without first moving them into a filing system.
what: Athena queries CSV, JSON or Parquet files in S3 using normal SQL. Nothing to set up. Store data as Parquet and partition it, or queries get slow and expensive.
when: You do not want a data warehouse yet
nope: Fast dashboards many people refresh all day. Use Redshift.
pay: Per TB of data scanned. Bad file formats cost real money here.
eg: Asking how many orders came from Gujarat last month, straight from log files.

name: Amazon EMR
one: Big data processing with Spark and Hadoop.
like: Hiring a hundred workers for one week to sort a mountain of paperwork.
what: EMR runs Spark, Hive and Hadoop clusters for heavy processing. It is powerful and needs real expertise. Most teams should try Athena or Glue first.
nope: Anything Athena can answer.
pay: Per instance hour plus an EMR fee.
eg: Reprocessing five years of raw logs in one run.

name: Amazon Kinesis
one: Handles data that never stops arriving.
like: A conveyor belt running all day. You take things off as they pass.
what: Kinesis takes continuous streams of events and lets several consumers read them in order. Unlike a queue, data stays for a set window so more than one reader can process it.
nope: A handful of events per day. Use SQS or EventBridge.
pay: Per shard hour, or per GB with on demand.
eg: Every page view on a site, flowing in live for a real time counter.

name: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka
Amazon Redshift
one: A warehouse built for asking big questions of big data.
like: A library with a proper index, built for research rather than for borrowing one book.
what: Redshift is a data warehouse. It answers analytical queries over billions of rows fast. It is not for running your app. You load data into it from S3 or your database.
nope: The live database behind your app
Small data. Athena is cheaper.
pay: Per node hour, or per unit with Serverless.
eg: A dashboard showing revenue by city by month across four years.

name: AWS AppSync
one: A managed GraphQL API.
like: One waiter who brings exactly the dishes you asked for, in one trip.
what: AppSync serves a GraphQL API backed by DynamoDB, Lambda or your own database. It supports real time subscriptions and offline sync, which suits mobile apps.
nope: You are happy with REST. API Gateway is simpler.
pay: Per million queries, plus real time minutes.
eg: A chat screen that updates live without polling.

name: AWS Step Functions
one: Draws your multi step process as a flowchart that actually runs.
like: A checklist that ticks itself, remembers where it stopped, and retries the step that failed.
what: Step Functions coordinates several Lambdas or services in order, with branches, retries and waits. It remembers state, so a long process survives failures. You can see exactly which step failed.
when: Anything that takes minutes or days
nope: A single function call.
pay: Per state transition. The Express type is cheaper for high volume.
eg: Order, then payment, then invoice, then email, with a retry if payment times out.

name: Amazon EventBridge
one: A router for events between services.
like: A post office that reads the address and delivers only to the right houses.
what: EventBridge takes events and sends them to targets based on rules you write. AWS services and some SaaS tools publish into it. It can also run things on a schedule, like a cron.
when: Many events with rules about who cares
nope: A single simple hand off. SQS is simpler.
pay: Per million events. Scheduled rules are free.
eg: Run a report every night at 2am IST.

name: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow
Amazon Simple Notification Service
one: Sends one message to many listeners at once.
like: A WhatsApp group broadcast. One post, everyone in the group sees it.
what: SNS publishes a message to a topic. Everything subscribed gets a copy: queues, Lambda functions, emails, SMS. SQS is one to one, SNS is one to many.
when: One event must trigger several things
nope: You need a durable work queue. Use SQS.
pay: Per million publishes, plus SMS charges which are not cheap.
eg: A payment succeeds, so an email goes out, stock updates and analytics record it.

name: Amazon Simple Queue Service
one: A waiting line for tasks.
like: A ticket counter. Work is dropped in the queue and picked up when someone is free.
what: SQS holds messages until a worker takes them. If the worker crashes the message comes back. It protects you from traffic spikes. Standard queues can deliver a message twice, so your worker must handle that.
when: Slow work that should not block the user
nope: You need an instant answer back to the user.
pay: Per million requests. Very cheap.
eg: Order placed, a message goes in the queue, invoices are generated in the background.

name: Amazon Bedrock
one: Use ready made AI models, including Claude, through one API.
like: A tap. The water treatment plant already exists, you just open the tap.
what: Bedrock gives access to foundation models from several providers without managing any servers. Your data is not used to train the models. It supports retrieval from your own documents and agents that take actions.
nope: A simple rule would do the job.
You need to train on your own data from scratch. Use SageMaker.
pay: Per thousand input and output tokens. Provisioned capacity is also available.
eg: Reading a scanned invoice and pulling out the amount and date.

name: Amazon Comprehend
one: Finds meaning inside plain text.
like: A reader who highlights the names, places and mood in a letter.
what: Comprehend pulls out entities, key phrases, sentiment and language from text. It also detects personal data, which is useful for privacy work.
nope: Complex reasoning. Use Bedrock.
pay: Per unit of text processed.
eg: Flagging angry support messages so they are answered first.

name: Amazon Polly
one: Turns written text into a natural sounding voice.
like: A newsreader who will read anything you hand over.
what: Polly converts text to speech in many languages and voices, including Indian English and Hindi. Neural voices sound noticeably better than the standard ones.
nope: You need a specific human's voice.
pay: Per million characters.
eg: Turning a written lesson into an audio file students can listen to.

name: Amazon Rekognition
one: Understands what is in a picture or video.
like: A person who can glance at a photo and tell you what is in it.
what: Rekognition detects objects, text, unsafe content and faces in images and video. Face features carry real privacy and legal weight, so check the law before using them on people.
nope: Reading a structured document. Use Textract.
pay: Per image or per minute of video.
eg: Automatically rejecting an uploaded profile photo that is not a face.

name: Amazon SageMaker AI
one: Build and train your own machine learning models.
like: A full workshop with tools, benches and machines, for making something custom.
what: SageMaker covers the whole machine learning lifecycle: prepare data, train, tune, deploy, monitor. It is for building your own model. If you just want to use an existing AI model, Bedrock is far simpler.
when: You have your own data and a real ML problem
nope: You want to use a ready made model. Use Bedrock.
pay: Per instance hour for notebooks, training and endpoints. Idle endpoints are a classic waste.
eg: Training a model on your own sales data to predict next month's demand.

name: Amazon Textract
one: Pulls text and tables out of scanned documents.
like: A clerk who types up a scanned form into a spreadsheet, including the table.
what: Textract reads printed and handwritten text, and understands forms and tables, unlike basic OCR. It returns structured data with a confidence score for each field.
nope: A clean digital PDF you can already read.
pay: Per page, more for forms and tables.
eg: Reading a scanned purchase order into your system.

name: Amazon Transcribe
one: Turns speech into written text.
like: A stenographer who types everything that is said.
what: Transcribe converts audio and video to text, with timestamps and speaker labels. It handles Indian English. Accuracy drops with heavy background noise or heavy code switching.
nope: Very poor audio. Fix the recording first.
pay: Per second of audio.
eg: Auto subtitles on a recorded class.

name: Amazon Translate
one: Translates text between languages.
like: An interpreter who works instantly and never tires.
what: Translate converts text between many languages including Hindi and Gujarati. Quality is good for general text and weaker on specialised jargon unless you give it a custom glossary.
nope: Legal or medical text where a mistake is serious. Use a human.
pay: Per million characters.
eg: Showing course descriptions in Gujarati as well as English.

name: Amazon Simple Email Service
one: Sends email from your app, cheaply and at scale.
like: A bulk post office for letters your system writes.
what: SES sends transactional and bulk email. New accounts start in a sandbox and must be approved for real sending. You must set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC or your mail lands in spam.
nope: A handful of manual emails a week.
pay: Per thousand emails. Very cheap.
eg: Emailing an invoice PDF the moment a payment succeeds.

name: AWS Cost Explorer
one: Shows where your AWS money is going.
like: A bank statement with charts, so you can see what you actually spend on.
what: Cost Explorer breaks the bill down by service, tag and time, and forecasts next month. Tag everything from day one or the breakdown is useless. Set a budget alert on day one too.
pay: The console view is free. The API has a small per request charge.
eg: Spotting that a forgotten test server has cost 4,000 rupees this month.

name: AWS App Runner
one: Give it your code or container, it runs a web service.
like: A vending machine for web apps. Put the code in, a running URL comes out.
what: App Runner builds from your repository or image, runs it, scales it and gives you HTTPS. No VPC or load balancer to configure. Less control than ECS, far less to learn.
when: Small teams with no ops person
nope: Complex networking needs.
pay: Per vCPU and GB while running, with a lower idle rate.
eg: A Node API live from a GitHub repo in minutes.

name: AWS Batch
one: Runs large numbers of background jobs.
like: A night shift that works through a pile of tasks while you sleep.
what: Batch queues your jobs and starts the right amount of compute to work through them, then shuts it down. It handles dependencies and retries. Good with Spot instances for cheap compute.
nope: A few small tasks. Use Lambda.
pay: Free service. You pay for the compute it starts.
eg: Generating ten thousand certificate PDFs overnight.

name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
one: Upload your code and AWS sets up the servers for you.
like: A serviced office. Bring your laptop, the desk and internet are ready.
what: Beanstalk takes your application and creates the EC2 servers, load balancer and scaling behind the scenes. You can still reach in and change things. It is an older service and newer options often fit better.
when: A traditional app you want online fast
You want servers without configuring them
nope: A brand new project. Look at App Runner or containers first.
pay: Free. You pay for the resources it creates.
eg: Deploying a Django app without touching a load balancer setting.

name: AWS Lambda
one: Run a small piece of code without owning a server.
like: A taxi instead of a car. You pay for the trip, not for parking it all night.
what: You upload a function. AWS runs it when something triggers it, then shuts it down. Nothing to patch, nothing running idle. It sleeps between requests, so the first call after a quiet spell can be slower.
when: Short jobs that run on an event
You do not want to manage a server at all
nope: Jobs that run longer than 15 minutes
Something that must respond instantly every single time
pay: Per request and per millisecond of run time. Nothing when idle.
eg: Someone uploads a photo, a function makes a thumbnail, then stops.

name: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
one: Adds servers when busy, removes them when quiet.
like: Calling in extra staff on a festival weekend and sending them home on Monday.
what: You set a minimum, a maximum and a rule. Auto Scaling adds or removes EC2 machines to match. It also replaces any machine that fails a health check.
when: You want automatic recovery from a dead server
nope: Steady, predictable traffic on one machine.
pay: The feature is free. You pay for the servers it starts.
eg: Two servers normally, six during a live class, back to two after.

name: Amazon EC2
one: A computer you rent in Amazon's data centre.
like: Renting a flat instead of buying a house. You pick the size, you get the keys, you install what you want.
what: EC2 gives you a full server. You choose how much CPU, memory and disk. You install the operating system and your software. You control everything, so you also maintain everything.
when: You need full control of the machine
You are moving an existing server to the cloud
Your software must run all the time
nope: You just want to run a small piece of code now and then. Use Lambda.
You do not want to patch servers. Use Fargate or App Runner.
pay: Per second the machine is on, by size. Stopped machines cost nothing for compute but the disk still costs.
eg: A shop's billing software that must run 24 hours a day on one server.

name: Amazon Lightsail
one: A simple server at a fixed monthly price.
like: A prepaid mobile plan. One price, known limits, no bill shock.
what: Lightsail gives a small server, a fixed price and a simple console. It hides most of AWS. Good for learning and small sites. You outgrow it once you need real AWS features.
nope: Anything that will need to scale properly.
pay: A fixed price per month, from a few dollars.
eg: A WordPress site for a small business.

name: AWS Fargate
one: Runs containers without you owning any servers.
like: Ordering food instead of renting a kitchen. You get the meal, not the gas bill.
what: Fargate is not a separate service you visit. It is a way to run ECS or EKS where AWS supplies the machine. No patching, no capacity planning. It costs more per unit than raw EC2.
when: You want containers with no servers to manage
nope: Very heavy steady workloads where EC2 is cheaper.
pay: Per vCPU and per GB of memory, per second.
eg: A background worker that runs for ten minutes each night.

name: Amazon Elastic Container Registry
one: A private store for your container images.
like: Your own locked shelf for the blueprints your factory builds from.
what: ECR keeps Docker images privately in your account. ECS, EKS and Lambda pull from it. It can scan images for known vulnerabilities.
when: You build containers and do not want them public
nope: Open source images that are fine on Docker Hub.
pay: Per GB stored, plus data transfer.
eg: Pushing a new build image, then telling ECS to use it.

name: Amazon Elastic Container Service
one: Runs your app in containers, the simple AWS way.
like: Standard shipping containers. Any port can handle them because the shape is always the same.
what: ECS runs Docker containers for you. It restarts them if they crash and can scale them. It is simpler than Kubernetes and only works on AWS.
when: You want containers without learning Kubernetes
nope: You need to run the same setup on other clouds too. Use EKS.
pay: Free control plane. You pay for the EC2 or Fargate capacity underneath.
eg: A Node.js API running as three containers behind a load balancer.

name: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service
one: Managed Kubernetes.
like: The international standard plug socket. It works the same everywhere, and the wiring is complicated.
what: EKS runs Kubernetes so you do not have to run the control plane. Kubernetes is powerful and genuinely hard. It is the right answer for large teams and the wrong answer for small ones.
when: You must stay portable across clouds
nope: A small team shipping one app. ECS or App Runner will hurt less.
pay: An hourly fee for each cluster, plus the compute underneath.
eg: A company running forty microservices across several teams.

name: Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS
AWS Database Migration Service
one: Moves a database into AWS with almost no downtime.
like: Shifting house while still living in it. Things move across one room at a time.
what: DMS copies an existing database into AWS and keeps replicating changes until you switch over. It can also change engine, for example Oracle to PostgreSQL, paired with the conversion tool.
when: Moving an on premise database to AWS
nope: A small database you can dump and restore in an hour.
pay: Per replication instance hour.
eg: Moving a live MySQL server to RDS with minutes of downtime, not days.

name: Amazon Aurora
one: Amazon's faster version of MySQL and PostgreSQL.
like: The same car, tuned. It drives the same way, it just goes faster and recovers better.
what: Aurora speaks MySQL and PostgreSQL, so your code usually works unchanged. Storage grows on its own and copies data across three availability zones. Serverless versions can scale down when quiet.
when: Traffic goes up and down a lot
nope: A tiny app. Plain RDS is cheaper.
pay: Per hour, plus storage used, plus reads and writes. Serverless charges by capacity used.
eg: A growing LMS where thousands of students log in at exam time.

name: Amazon DynamoDB
one: A very fast database with no tables to join.
like: A cloakroom. You hand over a ticket, you get your coat instantly. You cannot ask it which coats are blue.
what: DynamoDB gives single digit millisecond reads at any scale. You must know how you will look data up before you design it. Queries it was not designed for are slow or impossible.
nope: You need flexible reporting queries
Your access patterns keep changing
pay: Per read and write, or a fixed capacity. Plus storage.
eg: Storing which lesson each student is currently on, looked up by student id.

name: Amazon ElastiCache
one: Keeps frequently used data in memory so it is fast.
like: Keeping the tools you use most on the bench, not in the store room.
what: ElastiCache runs Redis or Memcached. It holds results in memory so your database is not asked the same question a thousand times. Memory is not permanent, so never keep the only copy here.
nope: Data you cannot afford to lose.
pay: Per node hour.
eg: Caching the course list so the database is hit once a minute, not once a click.

name: Amazon RDS
one: A normal SQL database, run for you.
like: A rented flat with a cleaner included. It is still your flat, someone else does the chores.
what: RDS runs MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle or SQL Server. AWS handles backups, patching and standby copies. You still design the tables and write the queries.
when: Normal business data: orders, users, invoices
nope: You need one database serving the whole world at once. Look at Aurora or DynamoDB.
pay: Per hour the database is on, by size, plus storage and backups.
eg: The orders table for a shop, with an automatic nightly backup.

name: AWS Amplify
one: The quickest way to put a web or mobile front end online.
like: A ready made kitchen fitted in a day, instead of building one.
what: Amplify hosts your front end, connects to GitHub and deploys on every push. It can also generate a backend with auth, API and storage. Great to start, restrictive once your needs grow.
when: React, Next.js or Vue front ends
nope: Complex custom backends.
pay: Per build minute and per GB served, with a free tier.
eg: Pushing to GitHub and the site is live two minutes later.

name: AWS CloudFormation
one: Writes your whole setup as a file, so you can rebuild it exactly.
like: An IKEA instruction sheet for your infrastructure. Same sheet, same result, every time.
what: You describe what you want in YAML or JSON. CloudFormation creates it, updates it, and can delete it all cleanly. No more clicking in the console and forgetting what you did.
when: You want staging and production to match
You want a record of your infrastructure
nope: A one off experiment you will delete tomorrow.
pay: Free. You pay for what it creates.
eg: One file that builds a VPC, two servers, a load balancer and a database.

name: AWS CloudTrail
one: Records who did what in your AWS account.
like: A CCTV log of the building. Not what the machines did, what the people did.
what: CloudTrail records every API call: who, when, from where. It is how you answer 'who deleted that database'. CloudWatch watches your app. CloudTrail watches your account.
when: Always. Turn it on the first day.
pay: One free trail of management events. Extra trails and data events cost.
eg: Finding out which user turned off a security setting last Tuesday.

name: AWS Config
one: Records how your AWS setup changes over time.
like: A logbook of every change made to the building, with the rules it must follow.
what: Config records the configuration of your resources and checks them against rules. It can tell you what changed and when, and flag anything that drifts out of policy.
nope: A single tiny project.
pay: Per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation. It adds up.
eg: Alerting the moment a security group is opened to the whole internet.

name: AWS Organizations
one: Manages many AWS accounts as one company.
like: A head office with branch offices. One policy, one bill, separate premises.
what: Organizations groups accounts under one payer, applies rules that even account admins cannot override, and keeps production separate from development. Separate accounts are the strongest blast radius control AWS offers.
when: More than one project or client
nope: A single personal learning account.
pay: Free.
eg: Separate accounts for dev, staging and production, one combined bill.

name: AWS Systems Manager
one: Manage all your servers from one place.
like: A facilities team with a master key and a maintenance schedule.
what: Systems Manager patches servers, runs commands on all of them at once, stores configuration in Parameter Store, and gives shell access without opening SSH to the internet.
when: More than a couple of servers
You want to stop opening port 22
nope: Fully serverless setups with no servers to manage.
pay: Most of it is free. Some advanced features are paid.
eg: Applying a security patch to twenty servers with one command.

name: AWS Trusted Advisor
one: Checks your account and suggests fixes.
like: A yearly service for your car. It lists what needs attention.
what: Trusted Advisor checks for wasted money, security holes, missing redundancy and hitting limits. A few checks are free on every account, the full set needs a paid support plan.
pay: Some checks free. Full set needs Business support or above.
eg: Flagging an S3 bucket that is open to the public.

name: Amazon CloudWatch
one: Watches your systems and tells you when something is wrong.
like: The dashboard of a car. Speed, fuel, engine warning light.
what: CloudWatch collects metrics, logs and alarms. An alarm can email you or trigger scaling. Log storage grows quietly, so set a retention period or the bill creeps up.
when: Always. If you cannot see it, you cannot run it.
pay: Per metric, per GB of logs, per alarm. Log retention is the usual surprise.
eg: Alert on WhatsApp when CPU stays above 80 percent for five minutes.

name: AWS Transfer Family
one: An SFTP server that saves files straight into S3.
like: An old style letterbox bolted onto a modern warehouse.
what: Transfer Family gives partners a normal SFTP, FTPS or AS2 endpoint, while the files actually land in S3. Useful when a bank or vendor will only send files the old way.
nope: You control both ends. Use the S3 API.
pay: Per hour the endpoint exists, plus per GB. The hourly charge runs even when idle.
eg: A bank drops a daily settlement file by SFTP, it appears in S3.

name: Amazon API Gateway
one: The front door for your API.
like: A reception desk. It checks who you are, stops rude visitors, then sends you to the right room.
what: API Gateway takes HTTP requests and passes them to Lambda or your servers. It handles authentication, rate limits, keys and versions. It adds a little delay and a per request cost.
nope: A simple website. A load balancer is cheaper.
pay: Per million requests, plus data out.
eg: A mobile app calling /orders, which triggers a Lambda function.

name: Amazon CloudFront
one: Keeps copies of your files near your users so pages load fast.
like: A local warehouse in every city instead of shipping everything from one factory.
what: CloudFront is a CDN. It caches your content at locations around the world. Users get served from the nearest one. It also absorbs traffic spikes and shields your servers.
nope: An internal tool used by ten people in one office.
pay: Per GB delivered and per request. There is a generous free tier.
eg: A course video watched from Ahmedabad is served from an Indian location, not from Virginia.

name: Amazon Route 53
one: The phone book that turns your domain name into an address.
like: Saving a contact by name so you never memorise the number.
what: Route 53 is DNS. It points yourdomain.com to your server or CloudFront. It can also register domains, check if your site is healthy, and send users to the closest region.
when: You own a domain and it points at AWS
nope: Your DNS is already fine at GoDaddy or Cloudflare and you have no reason to move.
pay: A small monthly fee per hosted zone, plus per million queries.
eg: kwickprep.com points at CloudFront, which points at S3.

name: Amazon Virtual Private Cloud
one: Your own private section of the AWS network.
like: A gated plot inside a big township. You decide the roads, the gates and who gets in.
what: A VPC is where your servers live. You split it into subnets. Public subnets can reach the internet, private ones cannot. Security groups act as a firewall on each machine.
when: Always. Anything you run sits in a VPC.
pay: The VPC is free. NAT gateways and data transfer cost money and surprise people.
eg: Web servers in a public subnet, the database in a private one so it can never be reached from the internet.

name: Elastic Load Balancing
one: Shares incoming traffic across several servers.
like: A queue manager at a bank sending you to whichever counter is free.
what: A load balancer sits in front of your servers. If one dies, it stops sending traffic there. It also handles HTTPS so your servers do not have to.
when: You want HTTPS handled in one place
nope: A single small server with little traffic. It is an extra monthly cost.
pay: Per hour, plus a usage unit based on traffic.
eg: Three web servers behind one address. One reboots, nobody notices.

name: AWS Certificate Manager
one: Free HTTPS certificates that renew themselves.
like: A licence that renews automatically so it never expires on you.
what: ACM issues and renews TLS certificates at no cost for use with CloudFront, load balancers and API Gateway. Automatic renewal removes the classic outage of a certificate expiring at midnight.
when: Any site with HTTPS on AWS
nope: You need the certificate file to install on your own server. ACM public certs cannot be exported.
pay: Free for public certificates used with AWS services.
eg: HTTPS on your domain through CloudFront, renewing itself forever.

name: AWS Identity and Access Management
one: Decides who can do what in your AWS account.
like: Keys for a building. The cleaner's key opens the store room, not the safe.
what: IAM holds users, roles and policies. A policy is a list of allowed actions. Give the least access that still works. Never use the root account for daily work, and turn on MFA.
pay: Free.
eg: A role that lets one Lambda function read one S3 bucket and nothing else.

name: AWS Key Management Service
one: Creates and guards the keys that encrypt your data.
like: The master key cutting machine, kept in a locked room. You can use the keys, you can never take them out.
what: KMS holds encryption keys. S3, RDS, EBS and others call it to encrypt your data. The key never leaves KMS. Every use is logged in CloudTrail.
pay: Per key per month, plus per request.
eg: All backups encrypted with a key only two roles may use.

name: AWS Secrets Manager
one: A safe for passwords and API keys.
like: A bank locker. Only the right person gets in, and there is a record of every visit.
what: Secrets Manager stores database passwords and keys encrypted. Your app fetches them at runtime instead of keeping them in code. It can rotate database passwords automatically.
when: Anything you would hate to see on GitHub
nope: Plain non secret settings. Parameter Store is cheaper.
pay: Per secret per month, plus API calls.
eg: The database password is fetched at startup, never written in the repo.

name: AWS Shield
one: Protection against attacks that try to flood your site.
like: Flood barriers around the building.
what: Shield Standard is automatic and free on CloudFront and load balancers. Shield Advanced is a paid tier with a response team and bill protection. Most small projects only ever need Standard.
nope: A small site. Standard is already on and free.
pay: Standard is free. Advanced is a large fixed monthly fee.
eg: A flood of fake traffic is absorbed before it reaches your servers.

name: AWS WAF
one: A filter that blocks bad web traffic before it reaches you.
like: A security guard at the gate who turns away known troublemakers.
what: WAF sits in front of CloudFront, a load balancer or API Gateway. It blocks SQL injection attempts, bad bots and abusive IPs, and can rate limit. It is a filter, not a fix for insecure code.
nope: Internal tools behind a VPN.
pay: Per rule per month, plus per million requests.
eg: Blocking an IP that tries two hundred logins a minute.

name: Amazon Cognito
one: Sign up and log in for your app's users, ready made.
like: Hiring a receptionist who checks ID, instead of building your own front desk.
what: Cognito handles user sign up, login, password reset, MFA and Google or Apple login. Your app gets a token. Do not confuse it with IAM. IAM is for your team, Cognito is for your customers.
when: You do not want to store passwords yourself
nope: You only need internal staff access. Use IAM Identity Center.
pay: Per monthly active user, with a free tier.
eg: Students logging into a learning app with email or Google.

name: Amazon GuardDuty
one: Watches for signs that someone has broken in.
like: A burglar alarm that has learned what normal looks like in your house.
what: GuardDuty reads your logs and flags suspicious activity: a key used from a strange country, a server talking to a known bad address, crypto mining. It only tells you, it does not block.
when: You want intrusion detection without effort
nope: A throwaway learning account, unless you want to see how it works.
pay: By the volume of logs analysed. Watch this one.
eg: An alert that your access key is suddenly being used from another continent.

name: AWS Backup
one: One place to schedule backups of everything.
like: One alarm clock for the whole house instead of one in every room.
what: AWS Backup sets backup rules across EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS and more, from a single policy. It handles retention and can copy backups to another region. A backup you have never restored is not a backup.
when: More than one thing needs backing up
nope: A single database whose own backups are enough.
pay: Per GB of backup stored.
eg: Daily backups kept 30 days, monthly kept a year, copied to Mumbai.

name: Amazon Elastic Block Store
one: The hard disk attached to your EC2 server.
like: The hard drive inside a computer, except you can unplug it and attach it to another computer.
what: EBS is a disk volume for one EC2 instance. It survives when the instance stops. You can take snapshots for backup. Type gp3 is the sensible default.
when: Any EC2 server needs a disk
nope: Sharing one disk across many servers. Use EFS.
Storing files for a website. Use S3.
pay: Per GB per month, whether or not you use the space. Snapshots cost extra.
eg: A 100 GB disk holding the application and its data.

name: Amazon Simple Storage Service Glacier
one: Very cheap storage for files you almost never open.
like: A deep basement archive. Cheap to keep things, slow to fetch them.
what: Glacier classes store data at a fraction of normal S3 cost. Retrieval can take minutes or hours depending on the tier, and costs extra. It is for archives, not for anything you serve live.
when: Records you must keep for years
nope: Anything a user might open today.
pay: Very low per GB per month. You pay to retrieve.
eg: Seven years of invoices kept for audit.

name: Amazon Simple Storage Service
one: A place to keep files, as many as you want.
like: An unlimited cupboard. You put a file in, you get a link to it.
what: S3 stores files, called objects, in buckets. It is built for very high durability. It is not a disk you can mount and edit in place. You put a whole file and get a whole file.
nope: A database. It cannot search inside your data.
A file share your server edits live. Use EFS.
pay: Per GB stored per month, plus requests, plus data going out.
eg: All product photos for an online shop, served through CloudFront.
